title: Which HTTP method do you prefer for passing sensitive data like Aadhaar/PAN (POST, body not URL)?
shortTitle: Preferred HTTP Method for Passing Sensitive Data (Aadhaar/PAN)
topicTitle: Which HTTP method do you prefer for passing sensitive data like Aadhaar/PAN

s1_definition.profdef: For sensitive data such as Aadhaar or PAN, I prefer POST (or PUT) and carry the value in the request body, never in the URL as a query parameter or path segment of a GET. This is because URLs are logged by servers, proxies, and browser history and appear in referrer headers, whereas a request body is not logged by default; combined with mandatory HTTPS/TLS, the body keeps the sensitive value off the easily-exposed surfaces.
s1_definition.analogy: Sending a National Bank of India customer's Aadhaar number in the URL is like writing it on the outside of an envelope — every post office, mailroom, and camera along the way can read it, and it stays in the mail log. Putting it in the POST body is like sealing it inside the envelope: the courier (HTTPS) still protects the whole thing in transit, but even the handling records only note "a sealed letter was sent," not the secret inside. So you prefer POST with the value in the body, not GET with it in the address.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** For sensitive data such as Aadhaar or PAN, I prefer POST (or PUT) and carry the value in the request body, never in the URL as a query parameter or path segment of a GET. This is because URLs are logged by servers, proxies, and browser history and appear in referrer headers, whereas a request body is not logged by default; combined with mandatory HTTPS/TLS, the body keeps the sensitive value off the easily-exposed surfaces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Sending a National Bank of India customer's Aadhaar number in the URL is like writing it on the outside of an envelope — every post office, mailroom, and camera along the way can read it, and it stays in the mail log. Putting it in the POST body is like sealing it inside the envelope: the courier (HTTPS) still protects the whole thing in transit, but even the handling records only note "a sealed letter was sent," not the secret inside. So you prefer POST with the value in the body, not GET with it in the address.

**One line to remember:** Use POST (or PUT) with the sensitive value in the request body over HTTPS — never put Aadhaar/PAN in a GET URL, because URLs are logged, cached, and leaked via history and referrers.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem with putting sensitive data in a URL is that URLs are pervasively recorded and exposed even when the connection is encrypted. A GET request typically carries data as query parameters or path segments, and those full URLs are written to web server access logs, proxy and load-balancer logs, CDN logs, and application logs; they are saved in browser history and bookmarks, they can be sent to third parties in the HTTP `Referer` header when the page links out, and they may be cached. TLS encrypts the URL in transit so a network eavesdropper can't read it, but it does nothing about all the places the URL is stored in plaintext at the endpoints. So even over HTTPS, an Aadhaar number in a query string ends up in logs and history that are a real breach risk and often fall outside the systems that protect the database.

A POST (or PUT/PATCH for updates) places the data in the request body. Request bodies are not written to standard access logs, are not stored in browser history, and are not leaked via the referrer header, so the sensitive value stays off those surfaces. Over HTTPS the body is also encrypted in transit. This is why the long-standing guidance, including from OWASP, is to never pass sensitive data in URLs and to use the message body instead. Semantically it also fits: operations that submit or change sensitive data are usually not the safe, idempotent, cacheable reads that GET is meant for.

Beyond the method choice, the senior view is that body-versus-URL is necessary but not sufficient — sensitive data needs defense in depth. You must use HTTPS/TLS everywhere (never plain HTTP), avoid logging the body fields that contain the sensitive values (mask Aadhaar/PAN in application logs), set `Cache-Control: no-store` so responses aren't cached, encrypt the data at rest and consider field-level encryption or tokenization so the raw Aadhaar is stored masked or tokenized, apply strict authorization and least privilege, and validate input. If a read genuinely must look something up by a sensitive identifier, you still send that identifier in a POST body (a "search" POST) rather than a GET query string, or you reference it by an internal non-sensitive id. The one-line principle is: sensitive values travel in the body of POST/PUT over TLS, never in the URL, and are masked in logs and protected at rest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India had a KYC verification endpoint implemented as `GET /verify?aadhaar=123412341234`. A log review found full Aadhaar numbers sitting in web server access logs and the load balancer's logs, and some in browser history on shared branch terminals — a serious data exposure even though the site used HTTPS. The fix was to change the endpoint to `POST /verify` with the Aadhaar in the JSON body, mask the field in application logs, and set no-store caching.

Our mini-project simulates both designs: a request router with a logger that records the URL (as real access logs do), showing that the GET design leaks the Aadhaar into logs while the POST design keeps the value in the body out of the URL log, and masks it in the application log — demonstrating exactly why POST-with-body is preferred.
sections.s4a_structure:
```

└── src/main/java/com/nbi/web/
    ├── HttpRequest.java

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two KYC verification requests, one a GET carrying the Aadhaar in the URL and one a POST carrying it in the body.

Step 1 — The GET request arrives as `/verify?aadhaar=123412341234`. The access log, like any real web server or proxy log, records the method and full URL — so the complete Aadhaar number is now sitting in plaintext in the access log, despite HTTPS protecting it only in transit.

Step 2 — The handler extracts the Aadhaar from the query string to process it, confirming the value genuinely traveled in the URL where it gets logged, cached, and saved to browser history.

Step 3 — The POST request arrives as `/verify` with the Aadhaar in the JSON body. The access log records only the method and the path `/verify` — the body is not part of standard access logs, so the Aadhaar does not appear in the URL log at all.

Step 4 — The handler reads the Aadhaar from the body to process it, showing the sensitive value stayed off the logged surface while still reaching the application.

Step 5 — For both requests the application log masks the Aadhaar to its last four digits, demonstrating the additional defense-in-depth measure, but only the POST design kept the full value out of the access log in the first place — which is why POST-with-body is preferred.

Final output:

```text
ACCESS LOG (what servers/proxies record):
  GET /verify?aadhaar=123412341234
  POST /verify

APPLICATION LOG (sensitive value masked):
  KYC verify for aadhaar=XXXXXXXX1234
  KYC verify for aadhaar=XXXXXXXX5678
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  GET (BAD):
    client ─ GET /verify?aadhaar=1234... ─▶ server
             │ URL recorded by: access logs, proxy/LB logs, browser history, Referer
             ▼ Aadhaar LEAKED into many plaintext stores (even over HTTPS)

  POST (GOOD):
    client ─ POST /verify  { "aadhaar": "..." } ─▶ server
             │ access log sees only: POST /verify   (body NOT logged)
             ▼ Aadhaar stays in body → over TLS in transit → masked in app logs

  Defense in depth: HTTPS + no-store + mask logs + encrypt/tokenize at rest + authz
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Request Handling for PII ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Boundary/Guard: sensitive values only in body, masked in logs     │
  │ Strategy: method dictates where the value is read from            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: handler verifies; AccessLog logs URL; masking separate        │
  │ O: new PII field = same body+mask pattern                        │
  │ D: handler depends on request abstraction, not transport detail  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Why POST body, not GET URL ──
  URL is logged  : web/proxy/LB/CDN access logs (plaintext)
  URL is stored  : browser history, bookmarks, cache
  URL leaks      : Referer header to third parties
  TLS caveat     : encrypts in transit only — not the logged endpoints
  BODY           : not in access logs / history / referrer → preferred
  also           : HTTPS + Cache-Control:no-store + mask logs + encrypt/tokenize at rest

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → handle(GET /verify?aadhaar=...)   [URL → access log LEAK]
  3.   → handle(POST /verify {body})       [access log sees only POST /verify]
  4.   → mask() in app log                 [XXXXXXXX1234]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
For sensitive data like Aadhaar or PAN I prefer POST, or PUT for updates, and I carry the value in the request body, never in the URL of a GET as a query parameter or path segment. The reason is that URLs are pervasively recorded and exposed even over HTTPS: a GET's full URL is written to web server access logs, proxy, load-balancer and CDN logs, and application logs, it is saved in browser history and bookmarks, it can be leaked to third parties through the HTTP `Referer` header, and it may be cached. TLS encrypts the URL in transit so a network eavesdropper can't read it, but it does nothing about all the places that URL is stored in plaintext at the endpoints, so an Aadhaar number in a query string ends up in logs and history that are a genuine breach risk and usually sit outside the systems protecting the database. A request body, by contrast, is not written to standard access logs, not stored in browser history, and not leaked via the referrer, and over HTTPS it is encrypted in transit too, which is exactly why OWASP's long-standing guidance is to keep sensitive data out of URLs and use the message body.

At the National Bank of India we found a KYC endpoint implemented as `GET /verify?aadhaar=...` had leaked full Aadhaar numbers into web server and load-balancer access logs and into browser history on shared branch terminals, despite the site using HTTPS, and we fixed it by switching to `POST /verify` with the Aadhaar in the JSON body. The senior point I always add is that choosing POST with the body is necessary but not sufficient — sensitive data needs defense in depth: enforce HTTPS everywhere, mask Aadhaar and PAN in application logs, set `Cache-Control: no-store`, encrypt the data at rest and prefer field-level encryption or tokenization so the raw value isn't stored, and apply strict authorization and input validation. Even when a lookup must be done by a sensitive identifier, I send it in a POST body rather than a GET query string, or reference it by an internal non-sensitive id. The line I always state is to use POST or PUT with the sensitive value in the request body over HTTPS and never put Aadhaar or PAN in a GET URL, because URLs are logged, cached, and leaked through history and referrer headers.
